Dear listfolk,

Stewart wrote back to ask a further question, which I thought may be
pertinent to those of you using mrds within Distance.

Stewart writes:

""
In reply to your and Eric's answers (below) I'm trying to do the right
thing now with respect to MRDS, so I've included a data column
'observer' populated with '1's after setting up a new project as double
observer. However, I get an error when trying to run MRDS:

[Observation].[Perp distance] AS distance
   [Observation].[object] AS object
   [Observation].[observer] AS observer
   [Observation].[detected] AS detected
   [Observation].[species] AS species
   [Observation].[person] AS person
   [Observation].[burnt] AS burnt
   [Line transect].[Label] AS label
   [Line transect].[Line length] AS line.length
   [Region].[Label] AS stratum.label
   [Region].[Area] AS area
   [Study area].[Label] AS global.label

**Error: Some values in the object field are not unique**

I didn't include a field called 'object' or 'detected' but it seems to
be trying to match it to my data.

I had a look at the help file and it seems that I may need to create
another two columns 'object' and 'detected' but this seems to be a bit
more than was suggested by yourself and Eric in previous answers. Is
this the case?
""

Indeed, Stewart is correct. Data for mrds require "object" and
"detected" columns. The object field should be unique to each
observation (so there should only be duplicated object IDs if you have a
double observer study) and the detected should be 1 if the object was
detected (again, 0s only occur in double observer surveys).

Further information can be found in the "Details" section of the ddf
section of the mrds R package manual
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mrds/mrds.pdf

I hope this is helpful!

best,
--dave

> mrds does expect an "observer" column in the data. The "partially
> matched" warning means that R means that you have some other column in

> matched the name (this is an R feature, so you can write "data$longvar"
> and get the contents of "data$longvariablenamethatidontwanttotype").
>
> So, in your case you might still have the wrong data in your model
> (though if the results are close, perhaps not). It's safest to create
> that extra column of all 1s to ensure that mrds is interpreting the data
> as single observer.
>
>
> Hope this helps.

messages.subject_clean: Increasing sampling with a systematic design?
messages.body_plain:
Hi group,

My question is about the best way to increase the sampling effort within a systematic design, once the survey is underway.

We are doing aerial surveys for ungulates. Often the areas have not been surveyed for quite some time, so we don't have a good sense of the density when we start flying, making it challenging to predict the necessary effort to achieve the desired precision. In the past, when we used a random design, it was easy to fly more transects if after a few days of flying we had not see enough groups (we would randomly order all the possible transects, and then just keep flying in the random order until we had enough... or ran out of money/good weather!). This year we would like to move to a systematic design to take advantage of its nice properties and possible improvements on precision. However, if after we fly our whole design, what happens if our sample size is too small, but we have more budge to keep flying? How to place additional transects in this case?

Thanks

messages.body_plain:
Hannah, yes, that is a downside of systematic sampling.  You need to know in advance how much effort can be completed on your budget, and select the spacing accordingly.  A half-way house is a possibility - decide on the maximum number of lines you can survey, say K, then divide your area into K equal-width strips.  Place a line in each strip (ideally a random start, followed by systematic spacing), then randomly re-order the lines.  Survey them according to this random order, until your budget runs out.  Precision should be intermediate between a simple random design with the same effort and a systematic design with the same effort.

Steve Buckland

Hi Nathalie and other listfolk,

Regarding the model failing to fit, this may be down to the sheer number
of covariates in the model. If you would like to send a minimal
code/data example to me I can investigate further. It may be worth
investigating goodness of fit tests/qq plots for these models (see ?ddf.gof)

1. How to perform a stratified analysis.

First, it's probably easier to write your model in Distance rather than
mrds (they end up as the same thing anyway, just Distance is a little
easier to read (though I am biased)). You can write your model as:

primates.cov2 <- ds(primates.covariate.fixed$data, key="hn",
	            formula=~as.factor(forest) + species+size +
	               mba.scaled + climber_perc + altitude.scaled,
		    truncation=90)

You can then write you data in the flatfile format (see ?flatfile) and
perform a "stratified analysis" as in
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/minke.html but here your
"Region.Label"s will be the species. Then when you call
summary(primates.cov2) you'll get the density/abundance estimates per
strata (ie per species).

This may or may not be biologically reasonable. (Others may want to
chime in on this...)

2. Interpretation of covariate effects.

This paper may be of use:
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/MarquesAuk2007.pdf pages 1234-1236.

Plots illustrated in the paper of covariate levels are not implemented
in mrds/Distance at the moment, though they are on my todo list.

3. Prediction outside of the sample from covariate values.

This is possible via the flatfile format by including rows where
distance is NA. However, if you think that environmental covariates (as
opposed to those that affect detectability) affect distribution, you may
want to consider density surface models (e.g.
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12105/abstract),
though this approach requires a relatively large amount of spatially
explicit data.

I hope this helps!

best,
--dave

That should be OK.  Personally, I’m not a fan of using adjustment terms in mcds.  They are there to put ‘wiggles’ in the detection function, if one of the key functions cannot fit the data well on its own, so giving greater flexibility.  Modelling covariates in the detection function also gives greater flexibility, and it’s not often that you get a big improvement in fit by including adjustments in addition to covariates, unless there are problems with the data (e.g. substantial rounding, responsive movement, etc).

>I'm assuming that while the estimation procedure does force the probability to be 1.0 a zero distance, the likelihood (and therefore the >AICc) is based on a general curve fitting procedure rather than restricting the maximum estimate to be no greater than 1.0 (especially >when using the cosine adjustment).

If you have no adjustment, this cannot occur, because the models for the detection function are non-increasing.  However, once you include adjustments, there is no guarantee that the fitted probability density function is non-increasing.  Because we obtain the fitted detection function by scaling the density function so that it is one at zero distance, that detection function might then increase above one.  The cds engine of Distance deals with this by incorporating a penalty term in the likelihood, that results in the fitted function being (almost) non-increasing.  The mcds engine does not have this feature.

Steve

Cds restricts probabilities <=1 by creating a grid across 0 to W and then enforcing g(x)<=1 at that grid.  You can do that with adjustments but if you then add in covariates which scale the detection function you would have to set up the grid over x for each covariate value.  That might be doable for a single factor covariate but imagine what would be needed with several factor covariates or worse a numeric variable.  Even if you then restricted it for each unique set of covariates in the data, that would not prevent a prediction for g(x) >1 for covariate values not included in your observed data.

I very much agree with Steve.  If you are using covariates then you are trying to explain what affects g(x).  When you use adjustment functions you are simply fitting for prediction without any attempt to explain. I'd go futher than Steve and say that I do not think the paradigms should be mixed.

Hi All,

I am working on line transect designs for aerial ungulate surveys. Last year we found that the precision of our density estimate was limited by high encounter rate variance. We flew 10 km random transects. I am wondering if 10km is too short, as we ended up with lots of transects with 0 detections, and I believe that this is the cause of our high encounter rate variance. I am considering lengthening the transects to 20 km for this year, although that leads to poorer spatial representation of the study area (as the number of transects is halved for the same amount of effort).

I am currently trying to use DSsim to investigate the effect of transect length on the cv(n/L) and cv(D), but I am a bit bogged down in getting the simulations to run at the moment, so in the meantime I thought I would poll the list to see if others can provide some guidance on the transect length vs number of transects tradeoffs, or papers that discuss this. I have read Saif et al (2012), which discusses this a little. They state that "the bias of estimates of density when using few long transects was less than when using several short transects, however, precision was lower." This is opposite of what I would expect... however, I did not think that in their simulations the difference in the number of transects between "few long" and "many short" was that great, nor were there many transects in either case (<20).

Any thoughts/previous experience on this topic would be very welcome.

Hannah

Hannah, no reason why changing the line lengths will affect either the precision or bias.  However, more, shorter lines give you greater replication, and hence better estimates of precision.  If you have high encounter rate variance, it is probably because your study animals tend to have a clustered distribution.  If you can predict where densities will be high, you may be able to reduce the encounter rate variance by stratifying your study area into high and low density, and estimate encounter rate in each stratum.  Or if there is a trend through your study area from high to low density, orient your lines so that each line passes through both high and low density areas.  This does reduce the encounter rate variance.

Hi Hannah,
I'll send you off the list a couple of papers where we look into encounter rate variance in detail.  Some brief thoughts in addition to what Steve said:

1. If you are using a random design, rather than a systematic design with a random start point, and if there are trends or clustering in animal density through your study area, then switching to a systematic design should have lower variance. You then need to be careful about how you estimate this variance in order to get the full benefit of the reduction. A quick way of adjusting for the systematic design in Distance is outlined in the PowerPoint slides I'll send you separately.

2. You discuss making your lines longer, suggesting that at present your lines aren't covering the full extent of the area of interest. If there are parts of your study area that your design is guaranteed not to sample, and if there's a chance that these unsampled regions might have different density from the sampled regions, you should address this if possible.

References:

Fewster, R.M., Buckland, S.T., Burnham, K.P., Borchers, D.L., Jupp, P.E., Laake, J.L., and Thomas, L. Estimating the encounter rate variance in distance sampling. Biometrics, 65, 225-236, 2009.

Fewster, R.M. Variance estimation for systematic designs in spatial surveys. Biometrics, 67, 1518-1531, 2011.

Best wishes,

Hello,

We are keen to test the MRDS approach for terrestrial line transects to monitor ungulates. Usually this method is applied for marine surveys on two different platforms. I was wondering if somebody has experience using this method in a terrestrial setting and ideally could provide some monitoring protocols?

We were thinking about a removal configuration as the only possible method (since the two observers would definitely cue each other on an simultaneous survey). We were thinking about Observer 2 is walking behind Observer 1. Observer 1 is not allowed to look behind in order to avoid any cues from Observer 2 towards Observer 1. As soon as Observer 1 detects animals he will stop and records everything to Observer 2. If Observer 2 observes additional animals missed by Observer 1 he/she will record it separately (standing some meters behind Observer 1), without giving any cues to Observer 1. We could also set the rule that Observer 2 waits to record (missed) animals just after Observer 1 passed them and Observer 1 is not allowed to count animals behind his/her position, so cues from Observer 2 towards Observer 1 will become irrelevant. With the latter approach however, Observer 2 may fail to measure the initial distance to the additional group detected (because he/she has to wait), so one methodical assumption would be violated.

Have you got any suggestions to overcome these problems and to develop a feasible monitoring protocol?

Many thanks for your support.
Lukas

Dear Lukas,
The approach you describe seems like a great way to help satisfy the g(0)=1 assumption (see everything on the trackline), but it is not a replacement for the independent observer platform condition in MRDS, because you've describe platforms that are dependent.  I'd propose that you pool them, and use CDS.  If you treat them as independent, you may get a qualitative sense of how many sightings Observer 2 picked up that Observer 1 missed, but as described, I don't think you should present it as a rigorous estimate of g(0).   That said, a first estimate of N, assuming g(0)=1 (and doing your best to satisfy that assumption) is a terrific start.  If you get the sense from your pilot study that violating the g(0)=1 assumption strongly influences your abundance estimate, maybe you could state that in your final report, and use it to leverage funding for a survey specifically designed to estimate g(0) in an unbiased, precise way.

I think you're doing  a good thing by addressing this.  I just wouldn't want you to misrepresent what you've done.  Many, many cetacean surveys are published assuming g(0)=1, because boat or crew limitations do not allow for independent teams.  It's fine, and even precautionary, but it's important to present it accurately.

All the best,
Rob

Hi Everybody

We are developing a framework for monitoring free roaming dog populations in the cities of Tierra del Fuego.

The objective is to monitor the mid and long term success of the policies to reduce free roaming dogs in the streets of the cities, like neuter and responsible pet ownership.

Cities are expanding in surface and adding new neigborhoods over the course of the years.

For that reason, and to avoid restrictions of design-based surveys, we are considering the use of Density Surface Models, also to be able to explain changes in dog presence by covariates.

Then, we should be able to tell the towns to follow a series of tracks (streets) that need to be surveyed over the years.

Adding covariates, we should be able to develop a DSM to assess abundance based on these covariates.

Then, here comest the two questions:

ONE:
The issue that comes to my mind and I want to share with you hast to do with modelling all over the space of the city, when free roaming dogs are distributed only along the streets.

The, the streets are like a mesh of something like 21m wide, separated by the about 800 blocks of around 90m side.

Potential solutions I was thinkg were:

1. Model the data as if they were collected and build a prediction grid where blocks can´t hold dogs (as if they are "0") meanwhile streets has a value of "1".

Then I wonder how much the smoothing all over the surface will affect the predicted results.

2. Model the data, but adding "dummy" transects located over some of the blocks, just to tell the model that inside the blocks   there are no dogs...

However the modelling may be affected  by the spatial spread of these dummy transects.....

3. Use something like the soap film smoother but I can´t figure out how we can handle such amount of  blocks...

TWO:

About detectability of dogs.

When travelling along the streets we need to record  dogs that can walk freely at the sidewalks or at the streets.

Streets has parked cars along the sidewalks, and many houses do not have fence, so dogs can sleep inside a parcel but leave the parcel boundarie as soon as they want to bark or whatever.

This impose visibility issues that affect detectability.

To reduce that I was thinking in make dogs more visible:
1. Survey the streets going behind garbage collectors, as these guys atract dogs either by their behavior (running along the streets) or leaving garbage behind ocasionally).
2. Broadcasting dog barks from the car meanwhile we go travelling.

I know that this affect the results of a survey, but if we want to see dogs in the streets I understand that we need to make them out

Any idea or previous experience in that is welcome. Many thanks

Adrian:

I won't speak to all of the issues you raise in the investigation of feral dogs in urban environments.  One think I will point out is the challenge of credibly dealing with the assumption that animals are distributed independently of the transects.

The distribution of dogs in the vicinity (0-200m) perpendicular from the transect is not uniform.  Dogs know exactly where your transect is located and they are either attracted or repelled by the transect (as you note in discussion of garbage trucks).  You may see some dogs walking down the centre of the street, but many will be hugged against the walls of buildings that line the street; then occasionally you will be able to see hundred of metres down a crossing side street.

As you know, distance sampling is based around fitting detection functions to sightings.  To fit those functions, you assume that the only thing causing the number of sightings to diminish with distance from the transect is caused by distance (not by parked cars or mounds of trash or garbage trucks).  Consequently the use of distance sampling methods in urban settings is challenged.

If you can model the manner in which the dog gradient changes at small distances from the transect, then you might be able to produce both a model of the detection function and a model of the animal gradient.  See Marques et al. 2013 (http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs10260-012-0223-2) for an example.  But as you can imagine the job is challenging.

messages.body_plain:
Distance sampling gurus:

Since there has been some pingponging on variance estimation due to transect length, I thought I would engage on another question that I have struggled with and hopefully get some thoughts from individuals with more experience and brain cells than I.

We have been doing point-transects, along specified 20-mile routes, in Texas for dove populations since the mid-2000s along secondary roads (please ignore discussion on bias in road-based surveys, but when a state is 96% privately-owned – you move on from those discussions). If anyone is familiar with the Mourning Dove Call-count Survey in the United States (now defunct), it is these routes that this questions pertains.  I recently gave a presentation on some preliminary results of the long-term data set on mourning dove, white-winged dove, and Eurasian-collared dove abundance in Texas. For background information, we estimate distances to each individual not cluster for this survey. To estimate abundance, we stratify each dataset into separate Texas ecoregions. We also pool data across years for estimation of the detection function, but let density vary by year to get an abundance estimate for each year. Standard enough based on the information I have gathered and discussions over the last 2 years (no prior in-depth knowledge of distance sampling prior to my current position).  An example of Bird Conservation Region (20; Edwards Plateau) and the current points that we do is below this email which will assist with the facilitation of discussion.

Currently, I pool all points across an ecoregion (or BCR) to estimate detection function, but then break out density by year to estimate population abundance (as said). For this to occur, I assume that all these points are independent of one another.  They are 1 mile apart which I think is fair enough for roll-up not too occur on the individual point transects. However, there may be some variance issues related to my current handling of the data. I wanted to get input form the group on 1) do you think I need to address this concern in variance estimation pointed out by others (whom I respect, but always good to get a second opinion much like MDs)?  2) if so, how would I approach this concern in either Program Distance or other?

I think this is rather complex and probably beyond  my current skill set, so wanted to get some input prior to forging forward. We are planning on doing a nationwide study using similar methods next year, and I wanted to get some of these details ironed out before simulating the number of points needed (20 per route) for each BCR across the United States.

Thank you for the time and reading this long-winded question, but wanted to be thorough in background, etc.

Cheers and hopefully some are enjoying leftovers from Thanksgiving today (at least my fellow Americans).

Hi Shaun,

As per your figure, it seems to me that strictly you should consider the points within each 20 mile route as non-independent, given that they clearly represent clusters of points across the landscape. Therefore, in terms of Distance software implementation, I would simply pool detections across points in the same route and use effort = number of points. If a given route spans across two different habitats (or ecoregions say) say, then I guess I would ignore the dependence across habitats just to keep it simple.

Apart from that, I think that pooling detections across years is a good idea if you do not have enough observations per year. Using covariates could help in that process too, in which you would have a MCDS detection function with detection probability being estimated by year (essentially a temporal strata) conditional on the observed covariates in said year.

Hope this helps, no Thanksgiving leftovers here in PT, but a sunny weekend ahead nonetheless!

cheers

Tiago

PS - As you requested, I've ignored the discussion (which is dear to me :) on bias from roads and assume that is accounted / considered / negligible...
